subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: The nurse is reading the night shift's report on a 79-year-old client admitted 2 days ago with heart failure who takes furosemide 40 mg daily. Highlight the findings that need the nurse's follow-up first.

segments.text: New crackles in both lung bases
Now needs three pillows to breathe at night

rationale.correct: Weight gain, new crackles and new orthopnea together point to worsening heart failure.

perOption.s2: Rapid weight gain suggests fluid retention.
perOption.s10: New orthopnea suggests worsening heart failure.
perOption.s12: This is not a clinical concern.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of deterioration in report.

questions.stem: The RN on a medical-surgical unit is reviewing roles with a new team. For each task, choose every staff member who may do it within the usual scope of practice. Each row may have more than one answer.

rows.text: Measuring the vital signs of a stable client
Giving an opioid by IV push
Reinforcing teaching that the RN started

rationale.correct: Scope differs by role; the RN keeps assessment, care planning and IV push medications.

perOption.r1:c3: This is a routine task for AP.
perOption.r2:c2: This is usually outside LPN scope in most states.
perOption.r4:c2: LPNs contribute data but do not develop the plan.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify scope for each team member.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a laparoscopic hernia repair this afternoon, and the consent form is on the chart unsigned. A nursing student asks who does what. Complete the nurse's explanation.

content.template: Before surgery, {{b1}} is responsible for explaining the procedure, risks and alternatives, and {{b2}} witnesses the client's signature.

options.text: the surgeon
the admitting nurse
the client's next of kin
a nurse
the client's adult child
the surgeon who explained it

rationale.correct: The provider explains the procedure; the nurse witnesses the signature and reports any sign that the client does not understand.

perOption.b1:a: The person doing the procedure obtains informed consent.
perOption.b1:b: Nurses do not obtain informed consent for surgery.
perOption.b1:c: This is not the family's role.
perOption.b2:a: Nurses often witness the signature, confirming it is the client's and given voluntarily.
perOption.b2:b: Family members are not the usual witness.
perOption.b2:c: The witness is usually a different person, such as a nurse.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse manager is reviewing three incidents from the past month with the unit's practice council. For each nursing action, select the legal term that best describes it.

cells.text: Telling a coworker false, damaging information about a client
Not checking a client's allergy before giving penicillin, causing anaphylaxis
Inserting a catheter after a competent client refused it

options.text: Slander
Battery
Negligence
Slander
Negligence
False imprisonment
Battery
Libel
Assault

rationale.correct: Know the common torts: slander, libel, assault, battery, negligence and false imprisonment.

perOption.b1:a: Spoken false statements that harm reputation are slander.
perOption.b1:c: Negligence is failing to meet the standard of care.
perOption.b2:b: A breach of duty that caused harm is negligence.
perOption.b3:c: Assault is a threat; here the contact happened.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client who lives alone in a two-story house is going home 4 days after a hip fracture repair with hip precautions and enoxaparin for 4 weeks. For each area, select the actions to include in the discharge plan.

options.text: Remove throw rugs from walkways
Install grab bars in the bathroom
Use a low chair without arms
Arrange home physical therapy
Book the first visit with the surgeon
Stop the enoxaparin once the pain improves

rationale.correct: Discharge plans after hip surgery cover home safety and follow-up services, and keep anticoagulation going as prescribed.

perOption.a: This reduces fall risk.
perOption.b: Grab bars support safe transfers.
perOption.c: Raised chairs with arms are safer after hip surgery.
perOption.d: This supports recovery of mobility.
perOption.f: Anticoagulants are taken for the prescribed time.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse on a respiratory unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with a chest tube whose drainage changed to 50 mL of bright red blood in the last hour
A client 2 hours after a bronchoscopy who has new stridor
A client with pneumonia whose temperature is 38.3 °C (101 °F) on day 2 of antibiotics
A client with asthma who is due for a scheduled inhaled steroid

rationale.correct: Airway threats come first; stridor after a procedure on the airway is an emergency.

perOption.a: This needs prompt follow-up, but it is under the 100 mL/hr threshold and less urgent than an airway threat.
perOption.b: Stridor signals upper airway obstruction, such as laryngeal edema or spasm.
perOption.c: Fever on day 2 of treatment is expected.
perOption.d: This is a routine dose.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN walks into a room and sees assistive personnel spooning food quickly into the mouth of a client who had a stroke, while the client lies flat in bed. The client is coughing. What should the RN do first?

options.text: Let the AP finish the meal, then report the problem to the manager
Stop the feeding, sit the client upright and coach the AP
Take over this client's meals for the rest of the stay
Write down what was seen so that it can be raised at the next staff meeting

rationale.correct: Supervision includes stopping and correcting unsafe delegated care immediately.

perOption.a: The client is at risk of aspiration right now.
perOption.b: This protects the client from aspiration and corrects the practice.
perOption.c: Coaching the AP is more effective than taking over the task.
perOption.d: Unsafe care needs correction now.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A competent 70-year-old woman tells the nurse that in her culture the eldest son makes health decisions and she wants him to decide about her treatment for breast cancer. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell her that the law requires her to make each decision herself
Confirm her wishes and document that she involves her son
Speak only with the client and leave the son out of discussions
Let the son decide even if she later disagrees with him

rationale.correct: Respect a competent client's chosen decision-making style, and keep checking that it is still what she wants.

perOption.a: A competent client can choose to involve others; insisting otherwise disrespects her preference.
perOption.b: A competent client may choose how decisions are made, including deferring to family.
perOption.c: This ignores the client's stated wishes.
perOption.d: The client's own choice comes first and can change at any time.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is in a residential program for opioid use disorder. A caller who says they are the client's employer asks whether the client is "in rehab for drugs." What should the nurse say?

options.text: "Yes, but the client is doing well and should be back at work soon."
"I'm not able to share information about anyone who may be here."
"Please call back after discharge, when I can tell you more."
"I'll ask the client to call you back as soon as possible today."

rationale.correct: Substance use treatment records have extra privacy protections; do not confirm or deny that someone is a client.

perOption.a: This discloses protected information.
perOption.b: Without written consent, the nurse cannot confirm or deny that the person is a client.
perOption.c: Disclosure is not allowed after discharge either, without consent.
perOption.d: This implies the person is a client here.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At handoff, the night nurse says a client 1 day after a hip replacement is "doing fine." Ten minutes later, the day nurse finds the client pale and sweaty, with a heart rate of 128/min and a blood pressure of 94/58. What should the day nurse do first?

options.text: Document that the handoff report did not match the findings
Assess the client further and call for help as needed right away
Call the night nurse, who has gone home, to ask what happened
Recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes to see whether they improve

rationale.correct: Always confirm handoff information with your own assessment, and act on what you find.

perOption.a: Care for the client comes first.
perOption.b: Act on what is found; the client may be bleeding or developing a PE.
perOption.c: This is not the first step.
perOption.d: Waiting delays care for possible shock.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Act on a change found after handoff.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with COPD and arthritis in both hands still cannot use a metered-dose inhaler correctly after two teaching sessions. The client presses the canister before breathing in and cannot hold the breath. Which team member can best help?

options.text: Respiratory therapist
Occupational therapist
Dietitian
Pharmacist

rationale.correct: Use the team member whose expertise matches the specific need.

perOption.a: Respiratory therapists are experts in inhaler technique and can suggest other devices, such as a spacer.
perOption.b: OT may help with hand function, but the inhaler technique and device choice are respiratory care.
perOption.c: A dietitian does not address inhaler use.
perOption.d: A pharmacist can help, but the respiratory therapist is the best fit for device technique.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: After report, the nurse has four clients to see. Place the clients in the order the nurse should see them, from first to last.

items.text: A client with a glucose of 62 mg/dL who is alert and able to swallow
A client with chest pain who took nitroglycerin 5 minutes ago and still has pain
A client who needs help walking to the bathroom
A client with a new tracheostomy who is coughing and has noisy, gurgling breathing

rationale.correct: Use the ABCs, then other urgent needs, then routine tasks.

perOption.a: The airway comes first.
perOption.b: Possible acute coronary syndrome is a circulation threat.
perOption.c: Treat promptly, but after the airway and circulation threats.
perOption.d: This can be delegated.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client received a tenfold heparin overdose. The quality team is starting a root cause analysis. Which question is the best place to start?

options.text: "Which nurse gave the heparin, and which nurse checked it?"
"What happened, and what in our process allowed it?"
"What discipline should the nurses involved receive?"
"Do we need to tell the client's family what happened?"

rationale.correct: Root cause analysis focuses on processes and systems, not on blaming individuals.

perOption.a: Starting with who blames individuals instead of finding causes.
perOption.b: A root cause analysis looks for the system factors that allowed the error.
perOption.c: Discipline is not the goal of a root cause analysis.
perOption.d: Disclosure is required, but it is not the question that starts the analysis.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client developed a large hematoma after receiving a double dose of enoxaparin. The provider and nurse are meeting with the client about it. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Say little about the cause to reduce the risk of a lawsuit
Explain the error honestly, what is being done and apologize
Explain that the pharmacy sent the wrong syringe, if that seems likely
Suggest that the client speaks to a lawyer before saying anything more

rationale.correct: Honest disclosure of errors, with an apology and a plan, is an ethical and professional expectation.

perOption.a: Hiding errors is unethical and often against policy and law.
perOption.b: Honest disclosure supports trust and is an ethical expectation.
perOption.c: Blaming others without facts is not appropriate.
perOption.d: This is not helpful and does not meet the duty to disclose.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client who lives alone is going home after a stroke and can walk only short distances with a walker. The client says, "I don't know how I'll get groceries or cook." Which resource is most appropriate?

options.text: A community meal delivery program
A speech therapy referral
Outpatient cardiac rehabilitation
A pharmacy delivery service

rationale.correct: Community resources, such as meal delivery, support safe living at home.

perOption.a: Delivered meals meet nutrition needs at home.
perOption.b: Speech therapy does not address getting food.
perOption.c: This is not related to the need.
perOption.d: This delivers medications, not meals.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN is making assignments for a day shift on a medical-surgical unit with one LPN. For each client, choose the most appropriate caregiver.

rows.text: Client with new atrial fibrillation started on a titrated diltiazem infusion
Client with stable chronic kidney disease who needs scheduled oral medications
Client being admitted from the emergency department
Client 3 days after a knee replacement who walks with a walker

rationale.correct: Assign unstable or new clients to the RN, and stable clients with predictable care to the LPN.

perOption.r1:c1: A titrated IV infusion and an unstable rhythm need RN care.
perOption.r1:c2: This is not appropriate for an LPN.
perOption.r2:c1: The RN could, but this can be assigned.
perOption.r2:c2: This stable client has predictable care.
perOption.r3:c1: The admission assessment is RN work.
perOption.r3:c2: This is not appropriate for an LPN.
perOption.r4:c1: The RN could, but this can be assigned.
perOption.r4:c2: This client is stable and predictable.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse on an endocrine unit receives four updates. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with hypothyroidism who feels cold and asks for another blanket
A client with Addison disease who is dizzy, with a BP of 78/44 and nausea
A client with type 2 diabetes who wants to know which snacks are allowed between meals
A client with Cushing syndrome who has new bruises on both forearms

rationale.correct: Signs of adrenal crisis need immediate action.

perOption.a: Cold intolerance is expected with hypothyroidism.
perOption.b: Hypotension, dizziness and nausea suggest adrenal crisis, which is life-threatening.
perOption.c: This is a teaching need.
perOption.d: Easy bruising is expected with Cushing syndrome.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis on a ventilator, who communicates with an eye-gaze board, asks to stop mechanical ventilation. The client has capacity and understands that this will lead to death. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that stopping a ventilator is not allowed in the hospital
Support the client's right and tell the provider about the request
Ask the client's family to talk the client out of the decision
Note the request and continue as before without telling anyone

rationale.correct: Competent clients can refuse life-sustaining treatment, and nurses make sure the request is heard.

perOption.a: A competent client may refuse life-sustaining treatment.
perOption.b: The request is taken seriously and passed to the provider for a full discussion.
perOption.c: This does not respect the client's autonomy.
perOption.d: Ignoring the request is unethical.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support a client's right to refuse treatment.

questions.stem: A handwritten order reads "Metoprolol 25 mg" with no route or frequency, and the nurse cannot read the provider's signature clearly. The client's next dose is due in an hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 25 mg by mouth twice a day, the usual route and frequency
Contact the provider to clarify before carrying out the order
Follow whatever the charge nurse thinks the provider probably meant
Leave the order for the next shift to sort out

rationale.correct: Clarify incomplete or unclear orders with the prescriber before acting on them.

perOption.a: Guessing what the provider meant is unsafe.
perOption.b: Clarification with the prescriber prevents errors.
perOption.c: Only the prescriber can clarify the order.
perOption.d: The order must be clarified before the dose is due.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is discussing professional accountability with new graduates. Which actions show professional accountability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reporting your own medication error
Keeping your clinical knowledge up to date
Practicing within your legal scope
Following up on care that you delegated
Signing for care that another nurse gave
Leaving the unit without giving a handoff

rationale.correct: Accountability includes honesty, competence, practicing within scope and following up on delegated care.

perOption.a: Accountability includes owning mistakes.
perOption.b: Competence is a professional responsibility.
perOption.c: This protects clients.
perOption.d: The RN remains accountable for delegated care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN case manager at a home health agency is planning this week's visits. Which visit can the RN assign to an LPN?

options.text: The admission visit and plan of care for a newly referred client
A weekly dressing change and data collection for a stable client
First-time teaching for a client starting insulin injections at home
A visit to decide whether a client's goals are met for discharge

rationale.correct: In home health, LPNs care for stable clients; RNs admit, plan, teach and evaluate.

perOption.a: Admission and care planning are RN responsibilities.
perOption.b: This is within LPN scope with RN supervision.
perOption.c: Initial teaching is RN work.
perOption.d: Evaluating outcomes is an RN responsibility.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse on a neurology unit receives four call lights at once. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury who has a pounding headache; BP 200/110
A client with multiple sclerosis who feels more tired than usual after physical therapy
A client with Parkinson disease whose tremor is worse because the next dose is 30 minutes away
A client with a migraine who asks for the lights to be dimmed

rationale.correct: Autonomic dysreflexia needs immediate action: sit the client up and find the trigger, such as a full bladder.

perOption.a: Autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency that can cause stroke or seizures.
perOption.b: Fatigue after activity is expected in MS.
perOption.c: Wearing-off before a dose is expected and not dangerous.
perOption.d: This is a comfort need.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who speaks only Portuguese is about to sign a consent form for a cardiac catheterization. The cardiologist explained the procedure in English and left. The client nods and reaches for the pen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Witness the signature, since the client nodded and seems to agree
Stop, and arrange for the cardiologist to explain it with an interpreter
Ask the client's 15-year-old grandson to translate the consent form for her
Use pictures and gestures to explain the procedure before signing

rationale.correct: Informed consent requires that the client understands, in their own language, through a qualified interpreter.

perOption.a: Nodding does not show understanding in a language the client does not speak.
perOption.b: Informed consent requires understanding, so the explanation is repeated through a qualified interpreter.
perOption.c: A child is not a qualified interpreter.
perOption.d: This is not enough for informed consent.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Ensure informed consent with language barriers.

questions.stem: The provider plans to discharge an 88-year-old client today. The nurse found that the client fell twice on the unit yesterday and cannot climb the stairs at home. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Discharge the client as planned and note the concern in the record
Share the findings with the provider and discuss the discharge
Tell the client not to agree to go home until the problem is fixed
Call the hospital administrator to stop the discharge from happening

rationale.correct: Advocate through clear communication of specific findings, then escalate if the concern is not addressed.

perOption.a: Concerns about safety must be raised before discharge.
perOption.b: Direct professional communication with specific findings comes first.
perOption.c: This puts the client in the middle of a team decision.
perOption.d: The nurse talks with the provider first, then uses the chain of command if needed.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is auditing the care of a confused client in soft wrist restraints who was pulling at a central line overnight. Highlight the actions that are unsafe.

segments.text: with a time-limited order from the provider
tied the restraints to the side rails
not offered fluids or toileting for 6 hours

rationale.correct: Restraints are tied to the bed frame with a quick-release knot, with regular checks and care for basic needs.

perOption.s4: Moving the rails can injure the client; restraints are tied to the bed frame.
perOption.s8: Basic needs must be met regularly.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with confirmed influenza A is on droplet precautions in a private room. No aerosol-generating procedures are planned. For each item, choose whether the nurse needs it for routine care.

rows.text: Gloves for contact with respiratory secretions

rationale.correct: Droplet precautions: a surgical mask on entering, plus standard precautions such as gloves for secretions.

perOption.r2:c1: This is not required for routine droplet care.
perOption.r2:c2: It is not needed unless an aerosol-generating procedure is done.
perOption.r4:c1: This is not required for droplet precautions.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is drawing up an IV insulin bolus when a family member interrupts to ask a long question about visiting. After answering, the nurse returns to the medication. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue from the step the nurse remembers finishing before the question
Start the preparation again and recheck from the beginning
Ask the client to watch and remind the nurse of the dose
Skip the independent double check this time to catch up

rationale.correct: After an interruption during a high-alert medication, restart the process from the beginning.

perOption.a: Interruptions are a common cause of error; memory is not reliable.
perOption.b: Restarting reduces the risk of an error caused by the interruption.
perOption.c: This shifts responsibility to the client.
perOption.d: Skipping a safety check is unsafe.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two clients on the same unit are named Robert Johnson and Roberta Johnston, and both are scheduled for morning blood draws. Which action best reduces the risk of a wrong-client error?

options.text: Use their room numbers to tell them apart
Add a name alert to both charts and use two identifiers
Move both clients into the same room so staff remember them
Call the clients by their first names only to make the difference clear

rationale.correct: Name alerts and two identifiers prevent wrong-client errors when names are similar.

perOption.a: Room numbers are not identifiers.
perOption.b: Alerts plus two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, prevent mix-ups.
perOption.c: This increases the chance of confusion.
perOption.d: A first name alone is not a safe identifier.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client started on zolpidem at bedtime has been found walking to the bathroom alone at night, unsteady on the feet. Which intervention is most effective?

options.text: Scheduled toileting before sleep and a bed exit alarm
Raising the side rails on both sides once the client is asleep
Turning off the night light so the client sleeps more deeply
Telling the client firmly not to get up at night without calling

rationale.correct: Combine scheduled toileting, bed alarms and lighting, and review sedatives in older adults.

perOption.a: These reduce unassisted night-time trips and alert staff when the client gets up.
perOption.b: Four rails count as a restraint and increase injury when clients climb over them.
perOption.c: Darkness increases fall risk.
perOption.d: Instructions alone are unreliable for a sedated older adult.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The power goes out on a medical-surgical unit, and the emergency generator starts. Which equipment should the nurse check first?

options.text: Ventilators and other life-support devices
The computer workstations used for charting
The electric bed controls in each client room
The nurse call system and the hallway televisions

rationale.correct: In a power outage, check life-support devices first and make sure they are plugged into the red emergency outlets.

perOption.a: Life-support equipment must keep working and be plugged into emergency power.
perOption.b: Charting can switch to downtime procedures.
perOption.c: Bed controls are not life-sustaining.
perOption.d: These matter, but they come after life support.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving capecitabine, an oral chemotherapy drug, to a hospitalized client with colon cancer. Which actions protect the nurse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear chemotherapy-tested gloves to handle the tablets
Leave the tablets whole rather than crushing or cutting them
Discard the packaging in the hazardous drug waste container
Wash hands with soap and water after removing the gloves
Handle the tablets with bare hands, since they are coated
Crush the tablets into applesauce if the client asks

rationale.correct: Hazardous drugs need PPE and safe handling even in oral form.

perOption.a: Gloves prevent skin exposure.
perOption.b: This prevents exposure to drug dust.
perOption.c: Hazardous drug waste needs proper disposal.
perOption.d: This removes any residue.
perOption.e: Coated tablets can still leave residue.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in a crowded clinic waiting room has had a cough for 6 weeks, night sweats and weight loss. Tuberculosis is possible. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Mask the client and move them to an airborne isolation room promptly
Leave the client in the waiting room wearing a mask until called back
Wear gloves when taking the client's vital signs
Ask the client to wait outside in the parking lot until called

rationale.correct: For a suspected airborne infection, mask the client and isolate them as quickly as possible.

perOption.a: Masking the client and isolating quickly reduces spread of a possible airborne disease.
perOption.b: This still exposes others in a crowded room.
perOption.c: Gloves do not protect against airborne spread.
perOption.d: This is not appropriate care.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old client with dementia keeps trying to climb out of bed and has no other way to communicate needs. Which intervention should the nurse try first?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint whenever the client is in bed
Low bed, floor mats and frequent checks on the client's needs
Raise the side rails on both sides to keep the client from getting out of bed
Ask for a PRN sedative to help the client settle for the night

rationale.correct: Use the least restrictive alternatives first, and look for unmet needs such as pain, toileting or hunger.

perOption.a: Restraints are a last resort.
perOption.b: Least restrictive measures reduce injury if a fall happens and address the reasons for getting up.
perOption.c: Clients may climb over the rails and fall from a greater height.
perOption.d: A chemical restraint is a last resort.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is about to start a unit of packed red blood cells and finds that the client's identification band was cut off during an IV restart. The client is alert, states the correct name and date of birth, and the second nurse is waiting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed, because the client stated the correct name and date of birth
Stop, have a new band applied per policy, then do the full check
Use the room number and bed label to confirm the client's identity
Start now and replace the band once the unit is running

rationale.correct: Never give blood without full positive identification, including a band on the client.

perOption.a: Transfusion requires a band on the client that matches the unit and the record.
perOption.b: Positive identification against a band on the client prevents fatal ABO errors.
perOption.c: Room and bed are not identifiers.
perOption.d: Identity is confirmed before the blood is started.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
